summary: Describes a scheme to packetize an H.263 video stream for transport using RTP. It also describes the SDP parameters for the H.263 video codec. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: H.263 video arrives as one long stream of compressed bits. This RFC explains how to cut that stream into RTP packets and how to mark each packet so a receiver knows where it can start decoding. The result is that a lost packet does not always break the picture.

subtitle: How H.263 video is cut into RTP packets, and how each packet says where it can be decoded from.

tldr.problem: H.263 video is delivered as one long compressed bitstream, but a network carries separate packets. Someone has to decide where to cut the stream, and how a receiver can start decoding again after a packet is lost.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a small payload header for each RTP packet. A P bit says the packet starts at a synchronization point, PLEN says whether a spare copy of the picture header travels with it, and an optional 8-bit field carries Video Redundancy Coding information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4629 is a Proposed Standard from January 2007. It obsoletes RFC 2429, updates the H263-1998 and H263-2000 media types registered in RFC 3555, and the text says new implementations SHALL use this format instead of RFC 2190, which moves to Historic status.

today: RFC 4629 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2007. It obsoletes RFC 2429 and updates the H263-1998 and H263-2000 media types in RFC 3555, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. Its text requires new H.263 implementations to use this payload format rather than the older RFC 2190.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4629 specifies an RTP payload header for video streams based on the 1998 and 2000 versions of ITU-T Recommendation H.263. The RFC calls the 1998 version H.263+ and the 2000 version H.263++. Because those two versions are a superset of the 1996 syntax, the same format also works for 1996 streams, and new implementations are told to use it in that case too.

The document replaces the payload format in RFC 2190, which some existing implementations still use for backward compatibility. New implementations supporting H.263 SHALL use the format described here, and RFC 2190 is moved to Historic status by RFC 4628. The document also updates the H263-1998 and H263-2000 media type registration that previously lived in RFC 3555, and it obsoletes RFC 2429.

Two things are defined: how to packetize an H.263 bitstream for RTP, and the SDP parameters needed to describe the codec in a session description.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC says how to carry H.263 video over RTP. It defines a small header for each packet, and it defines the parameters that describe the codec in a session description. It replaces RFC 2429 and takes over the media type registration that RFC 3555 held.

sections.title: New H.263 Coding Options
sections.content:
The 1998 version of H.263 added many coding options. Four of them change how the video must be split into packets: the slice structured mode, the independent segment decoding (ISD) mode, the reference picture selection mode and the scalability mode.

The slice structured mode was added for three reasons: better error resilience, a bitstream that suits a packet transport such as RTP, and lower video delay. It allows fragmentation at macroblock boundaries. Independent segment decoding breaks a frame into segments that are each decodable on their own, so damage in one segment does not spread to the others.

Reference picture selection lets the encoder point at an older reference picture instead of the previous frame, using the temporal reference as its identifier. The RFC makes no special provision for carrying back-channel information about decoder state, but says the Extended RTP Profile for RTCP-based Feedback, RFC 4585, MAY be used for that. Scalability comes in three kinds: temporal, signal-to-noise ratio and spatial. H.263++ added support for interlace mode and the definition of profiles and levels.
sections.plainLanguage: Newer versions of H.263 let an encoder split a frame into parts that can each be decoded on their own. This RFC explains how those options change the way the video is cut into packets, and which of them help when packets are lost.

sections.title: Carrying H.263 in RTP
sections.content:
The output of the encoder can be packetized directly. All bits of the bitstream, both fixed-length and variable-length codes, go into the packet, with one exception: when the payload of a packet begins with a Picture, GOB, Slice, End of Sequence (EOS) or End of Sub-Bit Stream (EOSBS) start code, the first two all-zero bytes of that start code are removed and replaced by setting an indicator bit in the payload header.

Three fields of the fixed RTP header carry special meaning here. The Marker bit is 1 when the current packet carries the end of the current frame and 0 otherwise. The Payload Type is assigned by the RTP profile for the application, or chosen from the dynamic range by the sender. The timestamp encodes the sampling instant of the first video frame data in the packet, and stays the same across successive packets when one frame occupies more than one packet.

The timestamp runs on a 90 kHz clock, the same clock used for H.261 in RFC 2032. Because both the RTP header and the H.263 picture header carry timing, the two must agree: the RTP timestamp and the temporal reference (TR) in the picture header must carry the same relative timing. Any H.263+ picture clock frequency can be written as 1800000/(cd*cf) source pictures per second, where cd is an integer from 1 to 127 and cf is either 1000 or 1001. The time increment between coded pictures is therefore an integer multiple of (cd*cf)/20.

Each RTP packet holds one H.263+ video packet. The layout is the RTP header, then the H.263+ payload header, then bytes of the compressed bitstream. The payload header is variable in length.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RTP packet holds one piece of H.263 video. The encoder's bits are copied straight in, except that the two zero bytes at the start of a start code are dropped and replaced by a flag bit, to save space. The RTP marker bit marks the last packet of a frame, and the timestamp runs on a 90 kHz clock that must agree with the timing inside the video itself.

sections.title: The H.263+ Payload Header
sections.content:
The payload header is always present and is of variable length. It starts with a 16-bit general header, which may be followed by an 8-bit Video Redundancy Coding (VRC) field and, when PLEN is greater than zero, by an extra picture header of PLEN bytes. The minimum length of the payload header is 16 bits, with PLEN equal to 0 and no VRC information present.

The general header holds four fields. RR is 5 reserved bits that SHALL be zero and MUST be ignored by receivers. P is one bit that indicates a picture, picture segment (GOB or slice) or video sequence end (EOS or EOSBS) start; two zero bytes must then be prefixed to the payload to rebuild a complete start code, so the bit removes two bytes from every such packet. V is one bit that indicates the presence of the 8-bit VRC field. PLEN is 6 bits giving the length in bytes of the extra picture header, and PEBIT is 3 bits giving the number of bits to ignore in the last byte of that picture header. If PLEN is zero, PEBIT is also zero.

The optional VRC extension holds three fields. TID is a 3-bit thread ID, and up to 7 threads are allowed. Each frame of VRC data uses as reference information only sync frames or frames within the same thread, and thread 0 is the canonical thread from which the sync frame should ideally be used. Trun is a 4-bit number that counts packets within each thread and increases monotonically modulo 16. S is a bit that marks the packet as carrying a sync frame.

Video Redundancy Coding works by running several independent threads of inter-frame predicted pictures. Damage to a frame then distorts only its own thread. From time to time all threads converge on a sync frame, an INTRA picture or a non-INTRA picture represented redundantly in several threads, and from that frame the threads start again. An encoder may send several representations of the same sync picture so that at least one copy arrives in at least one thread. When nothing is lost, the thread 0 copy is used and the others are discarded; packets with lower thread numbers have a higher processing and delivery priority.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet starts with a 16-bit header. The P bit says the packet begins at a point where decoding can start. The V bit says an extra byte follows for Video Redundancy Coding, which runs several copies of the video so that damage in one copy does not spoil the others. The PLEN and PEBIT fields say whether a spare copy of the picture header is attached and how many bits of its last byte to ignore.

sections.title: Packetization Schemes
sections.content:
A picture segment packet starts at the location of a Picture, GOB or slice start code in the bitstream, and always has P=1. An extra picture header can sometimes be attached; whenever PLEN is greater than zero, only the last six bits of the picture start code, 100000, are included in it, so a complete byte-aligned picture header can be rebuilt at the receiver by prepending the sixteen leading zero bits.

A sequence ending packet starts at an EOS or EOSBS code. It always has P=1 and PLEN=0. The RFC warns that some decoders read the loss of a packet holding only EOS or EOSBS information as the loss of essential video data and may then stop displaying later video, and it discourages encoders from sending EOS and EOSBS at all.

A Follow-on Packet holds bytes of coded data that do not start at a synchronization point, and always has P=0. Because it does not start at a synchronization point, its first bytes are not independently decodable. If the preceding packet is lost, the receiver may discard that Follow-on Packet and the ones after it, unless it scans the payload interior for a start code it can use to resynchronize.

There is no syntactic difference between the packet types beyond the P bit. The type is worked out from the P bit, PLEN and the first six bits of the payload. When the whole coded picture fits in one packet of reasonable size, which often happens for small formats such as QCIF with packet sizes around 1500 bytes, only a picture segment packet is needed. If it does not fit, either Follow-on Packets carry the rest of the picture, which costs the least overhead but adds no error resilience, or the picture is broken into smaller segments using the slice or GOB mechanism, each of which offers a synchronization point and can carry a redundant picture header so that decoding survives the loss of the packet holding the original picture header.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet that starts at a picture, slice or group-of-blocks start code can be decoded on its own, so it carries P=1. A follow-on packet holds the middle of a picture, so it carries P=0 and cannot be decoded on its own. Splitting a picture into smaller pieces at slice boundaries costs a little overhead but lets the receiver carry on after a lost packet.

sections.title: Media Type Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media types video/H263-1998 and video/H263-2000, updating the versions previously registered in RFC 3555. Neither has required parameters. The optional parameters select optional features of the codec and are written as a semicolon-separated list of parameter=value pairs.

For H263-1998, the picture size parameters SQCIF, QCIF, CIF, CIF4 and CIF16 each carry a Minimum Picture Interval (MPI). Permissible values are integers from 1 to 32, which correspond to a maximum frame rate of 30/(1.001 times the specified value) frames per second. CUSTOM takes three comma-separated values, Xmax, Ymax and MPI, where Xmax and Ymax give the number of pixels on each axis and must be evenly divisible by 4. A system that declares support of a specific MPI for one resolution implicitly supports a lower resolution with the same MPI.

A list of optional annex parameters says which parts of H.263 are supported: F, I, J, T, K, N and P. If no annex is specified, the stream is Baseline H.263. K takes one of four values describing the slice mode, from 1 (Slices In Order, Non-Rectangular) to 4 (Slices Not Ordered, Rectangular). N takes one of four values for reference picture selection: 1 (NEITHER, no back-channel data), 2 (ACK only), 3 (NACK only) and 4 (ACK+NACK). P describes reference picture resampling with four submodes.

PAR sets the width:height ratio as two colon-separated integers between 0 and 255, with a default ratio of 12:11. CPCF is a comma-separated list of eight parameters for a custom picture clock frequency and the MPI for each supported picture size, using the same 1800000/(cd*cf) formula, with MPI values from 1 to 2048 and an MPI of 0 meaning that picture size is not supported. BPP is the maximum number of bits, in units of 1024 bits, allowed for a single picture, an integer from 0 to 65536. HRD signals support of the Hypothetical Reference Decoder.

For H263-2000, PROFILE is an H.263 profile number in the range 0 through 10, and LEVEL is a level of bitstream operation in the range 0 through 100, describing the computational complexity of decoding. Support of any level other than level 45 implies support of all lower levels, and support of level 45 implies support of level 10. A system that specifies a PROFILE MUST specify the supported LEVEL, and PROFILE and LEVEL SHALL NOT be used with the other optional parameters. INTERLACE signals support for interlace display mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The media type names the codec and carries optional parameters. Picture size parameters say how often the sender can send frames at each size. Annex parameters say which parts of H.263 the receiver can decode, such as slices or reference picture selection. The H263-2000 type adds a profile number and a level that describe the decoder's capability.

sections.title: SDP Usage and the Offer/Answer Model
sections.content:
The media types map onto the Session Description Protocol, RFC 4566, in a fixed way. The media name in the m= line MUST be video. The encoding name in the a=rtpmap line MUST be H263-1998 or H263-2000. The clock rate in the a=rtpmap line MUST be 90000. Any optional parameters MUST be included in the a=fmtp line as a semicolon-separated list of parameter=value pairs.

With the offer/answer model of RFC 3264, the codec options F, I, J, K, N, P and T MUST NOT appear unless the sender of those SDP parameters can decode those options, because these options describe receiver capabilities even in a sendonly offer. An offer of a profile means the offerer can decode a stream using that profile; an answerer SHALL NOT change the profile parameter and MUST reject a payload type with an unsupported profile. The LEVEL in an offer gives the highest complexity the offerer can decode, and an answerer MAY change it. The INTERLACE parameter MAY be included in either offer or answer, independently.

Picture sizes and their MPIs can be advertised together or as a subset, and parameters offered first are the most preferred picture mode. For example, the string CIF=4;QCIF=3;SQCIF=2;CUSTOM=360,240,2 says the encoder should send CIF, which the receiver can decode at MPI=4, then QCIF at MPI 3, then SQCIF at MPI 2, and that the receiver can decode a custom size of 360x240 at MPI 2. If a receiver does not specify the picture size or MPI parameter, it SHOULD be ready to receive QCIF resolution with MPI=1. In multicast sessions an answerer SHALL NOT change any parameter in an answer; if the values are not supported, the payload type MUST be rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: In a session description, the media line says video, the encoding name says which H.263 version is used, and the clock rate is 90000. The optional parameters go on the format-parameters line. In an offer and answer exchange, the answerer must not change the profile and must reject a profile it cannot decode, while the level may be lowered to what the answerer can handle.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets using this payload format are subject to the security considerations in the RTP specification, RFC 3550, and in any applicable RTP profile such as RFC 3551. Confidentiality of the media stream is achieved by encryption. Because the compression used with this payload format runs end to end, encryption may be applied after compression, so the two operations do not conflict.

The RFC also notes a denial-of-service risk. A compression technique with a non-uniform computational load at the receiver lets an attacker inject datagrams that are expensive to decode and overload the receiver. The use of authentication of at least the RTP packet is RECOMMENDED. As with any IP-based protocol, a receiver may be overloaded simply by receiving too many packets, wanted or unwanted. Network-layer authentication can discard packets from undesired sources, although the processing cost of the authentication itself may be too high. A security review of this payload format found no additional considerations beyond those in the RTP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing in this payload format weakens the security of RTP itself, so the usual RTP rules apply: encrypt the media if it must stay private. One extra risk is that an attacker can send carefully chosen video data that is slow to decode, so the RFC recommends authenticating the packets.

viz.caption: THE 16-BIT GENERAL H.263+ PAYLOAD HEADER (RFC 4629 SECTION 5.1)

fields.name: RR
fields.desc: Reserved bits. SHALL be zero and MUST be ignored by receivers.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: 1 when the packet starts a picture, a GOB or slice, or a sequence end; the two zero bytes of the start code are omitted.

fields.name: V
fields.desc: 1 when the 8-bit Video Redundancy Coding field follows.

fields.name: PLEN
fields.desc: Length in bytes of the extra picture header; 0 when none is attached.

fields.name: PEBIT
fields.desc: Number of bits to ignore in the last byte of the extra picture header; 0 when PLEN is 0.

viz.caption: THE OPTIONAL 8-BIT VRC HEADER EXTENSION (RFC 4629 SECTION 5.2)

fields.name: TID
fields.desc: Thread ID. Up to 7 threads are allowed; thread 0 is the canonical thread.

fields.name: Trun
fields.desc: Packet number within the thread, increasing monotonically modulo 16.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: 1 when the packet content is for a sync frame.

viz.caption: HOW A RECEIVER TELLS THE PACKET TYPES APART

items.label: Picture
items.desc: The typical picture packet: a picture start code with no extra picture header.

items.label: Picture
items.desc: A picture with a complete picture header attached; check the UFEP field.

items.label: GOB/Slice/EOS/EOSBS
items.desc: Starts at a group-of-blocks, slice or sequence end code.

items.label: GOB/Slice
items.desc: Starts at a group-of-blocks or slice code and carries an extra picture header.

items.label: Follow-on
items.desc: The rest of a picture; it does not start at a synchronization point.

items.label: Follow-on
items.desc: A follow-on packet with an extra picture header, which allows resynchronization inside the packet.
